title: Use of acellular fish skin to improve wound healing after dermatological procedures
summary: In recent years, more and more people have required surgery for skin tumors or chronic wounds—both in hospitals and outpatient settings. Older patients and those with multiple health conditions often need careful and personalized wound care after such procedures, as their healing process is frequently impaired. In cases of larger skin defects, standard treatments such as skin grafts or local flaps are not always sufficient and can lead to complications like poor scar formation. A new material derived from the skin of the North Atlantic cod—known as acellular fish skin—has shown promising properties: it supports wound healing, reduces inflammation, and promotes skin cell growth. Until now, this material has mainly been used for treating burn and diabetic wounds. However, its use in dermatologic surgery is still largely unexplored. A clinical study is now underway to investigate whether fish skin can also improve healing after dermatologic surgical procedures.

interventions.name: Wound treatment with acellular fish skin
Wound treatment with standard of care (SOC)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients undergo a dermatologic surgical intervention requiring the use of a skin substitute.
Exclusion criteria:
Patients with acute untreated infections
Patients with metastatic cancer
Pregnancy
Breastfeeding
Known fish allergy
